14780: To snipe means to attack from a hidden or safe position, with precision, in a way that is hard for the target to defend against or respond to. That idea — hidden, precise, one-sided — runs through every use of this word.

To snipe originally means to shoot at a target from a concealed, distant position, usually with a high-accuracy rifle. The person doing this is called a sniper.

The key elements are:

  • Distance — the shooter is far away.
  • Concealment — the shooter is hidden; the target cannot easily see them.
  • Precision — it is a careful, aimed shot, not random firing.
  • Vulnerability — the target has little warning and little chance to fight back.

"Enemy soldiers were sniped at from rooftops as they moved through the street."

Because of those same qualities — hidden, one-sided, targeted — to snipe also means to make sharp, critical, or mean remarks about someone, especially in a petty or constant way.

It carries a specific flavor: the person sniping is usually doing it from a "safe" position — behind someone's back, through sarcasm, in a low-key way, or indirectly — rather than confronting the person openly and directly. It is criticism that stings but is hard to fully call out, because it is delivered in a sneaky or cowardly way.

"She kept sniping at her colleague's ideas during the meeting instead of offering real feedback."

"He spent the whole dinner sniping at his brother's choices in life."

"The politician's rivals sniped at him on social media rather than debating him face to face."

Notice that in all these examples, the "attacker" is not standing up and making a bold, direct statement. They are taking little shots from a safe distance — that is the essence of sniping in this sense.

If someone does this repeatedly, we might say they are constantly sniping or that they are a sniper (in a figurative sense). It suggests the person is picking at someone, chipping away with small but pointed criticisms, often out of jealousy, resentment, or a desire to undermine without full commitment to open conflict.

A very common modern use: in online auctions (like eBay), to snipe means to place your bid at the very last possible second before the auction closes, so other bidders have no time to outbid you.

"He sniped the auction with just three seconds left and won the item for a low price."

Why is this called sniping? Because, just like a military sniper, you are:

  • Waiting patiently and watching from a distance while others bid.
  • Striking at precisely the right moment — the last second.
  • Giving your target (other bidders) no chance to respond — there is no time left for them to raise their bid.

There is even software called a sniper tool that automatically places a bid in the final seconds of an auction on your behalf. The act itself is called auction sniping.

In informal sports language, especially in hockey, soccer, and basketball, to snipe means to score with a very precise, powerful, impressive shot — hitting exactly the spot you aimed for, leaving the goalkeeper or defender no chance.

"He received the pass and sniped it right into the top corner of the net."

"She sniped a goal from outside the box."

The word is used here with admiration. A player who does this regularly is called a sniper — someone known for clinical, precise finishing. This use keeps the idea of "precise targeting" but drops the negative or covert connotation. It is simply about deadly accuracy.

No matter which context you see it in, the word to snipe always carries these ideas:

  • Precision — not a random attack, but a targeted one.
  • A power imbalance — the sniper has an advantage; the target is vulnerable.
  • Limited ability to respond — the target is caught off guard, with little time or ability to fight back.
  • Often, some element of concealment or patience — the sniper waits for the right moment, or attacks from safety.

When these ideas describe a physical shot, it is literal sniping. When they describe verbal criticism, it is figurative sniping. When they describe an auction tactic, it is strategic sniping. Same word, same soul.

ContextWhat it means
Military / literalShoot at someone from a hidden, distant position
Everyday speechMake petty, pointed criticisms from a "safe" position
Online auctionsBid at the very last second, giving others no time to respond
Sports (slang)Score with a precise, powerful shot

When someone says another person is sniping at them (in conversation), it almost always carries a negative or frustrated tone. It implies the sniping is unfair, cowardly, or annoying — because the sniper won't just say what they mean directly. You would not describe a brave, direct critic as sniping. You reserve that word for someone who takes cheap shots.
14781: A sniper is a highly skilled shooter who fires at targets from a hidden position at a long distance, with extreme precision. The three pillars — concealment, distance, and accuracy — are what separate a sniper from an ordinary shooter.

1. Hidden
A sniper does not stand in the open and shoot. They hide — behind bushes, inside a building, on a rooftop, in a ditch, or camouflaged in tall grass. The target often has no idea where the sniper is, or even that a sniper exists nearby. This secrecy is central to what a sniper does.

2. Far Away
A sniper operates from a great distance — sometimes hundreds of metres, sometimes over a kilometre away. This distance protects the sniper and makes it very difficult for the target to detect or retaliate.

3. Precise
A sniper does not spray bullets randomly. They wait, aim carefully, and fire one precise shot intended to hit a very specific target. The goal is accuracy, not volume of fire. A sniper is trained to account for wind, distance, gravity, and even their own breathing before pulling the trigger.

In warfare and the military
This is the most common and literal use of the word. Militaries around the world train snipers as a specialised role. In a battle or conflict, a sniper might be positioned far from the front line, eliminating high-value targets (such as enemy commanders or machine-gun operators), disrupting enemy movements, or gathering information — all without being seen. Because one skilled sniper can change the course of a battle by targeting key individuals from a distance, they are considered a powerful and feared element of modern warfare.

In law enforcement
Police and counter-terrorism units also use snipers. For example, during a hostage situation, a police sniper may be positioned at a distance, ready to neutralise a threat with a single precise shot if lives are in danger. The objective is the same: accuracy from a hidden, distant location.

• Patience — A sniper may lie still for hours, or even days, waiting for exactly the right moment to act.
  • Discipline — They resist the urge to act prematurely. Timing matters as much as accuracy.
  • Training — Becoming a sniper requires extensive, specialised training in marksmanship, camouflage, map reading, and mental endurance.
  • A sniper rifle — Snipers typically use a long-barrelled rifle with a telescopic sight (scope), which magnifies distant targets and allows for precise aiming. This is very different from the short-range weapons carried by ordinary soldiers.

The word "sniper" is also used outside of warfare to describe a person who attacks, criticises, or undermines others in a sneaky, indirect way — without openly confronting them. Just like a military sniper strikes from hiding, a figurative sniper takes aim at someone from a position of safety or anonymity.

Examples:

  • "He was a political sniper, leaking damaging information about his rivals without ever showing his face."
  • "She faced constant snipers in the media who picked apart every word she said."
  • In online contexts, someone who throws sharp, targeted insults from behind a screen — without engaging in a direct argument — might be called a sniper.

The feeling conveyed is always the same: a hidden attacker making precise, damaging strikes from a distance.
How to Use the Word in Sentences

• "A sniper was positioned on the roof to protect the president during the visit."
  • "The enemy sniper had been hiding in the ruins for three days before anyone noticed."
  • "He wasn't the type to argue openly — he was a sniper, always striking when you least expected it."
  • "The military unit was pinned down by a lone sniper they couldn't locate."

To summarise: a sniper (noun) is someone who shoots with great precision from a concealed and distant position. In its literal sense, it refers to a trained military or law enforcement shooter. In its figurative sense, it describes anyone who makes stealthy, targeted attacks — verbal, political, or otherwise — from a position of safety or anonymity. The word always carries the sense of precision, concealment, and striking from a distance.
14782: A snippet is a small piece of something — specifically, a brief portion that has been taken or pulled out from something larger. The two ideas baked into this word are smallness and origin: a snippet is never the whole thing; it always comes from a bigger source.

Imagine you're reading a long novel. You mark one interesting paragraph and share it with a friend. That paragraph is a snippet — a small extract from the larger whole.

The same logic applies everywhere: a snippet of a song is a few seconds pulled from the full track. A snippet of a conversation is a brief exchange from a longer discussion. A snippet of news is a small piece of information from a larger story.

A snippet is not random or accidental. It's usually deliberately chosen — to share, to preview, or to highlight something worth noticing.

In everyday speech and media, this is the most common use:

  • "I only caught a snippet of what they were saying." (a brief bit of a conversation)
  • "The trailer shows just a snippet of the film." (a short preview clip)
  • "She read us a snippet from her upcoming book." (a small passage)
  • "I heard a snippet of that song and got hooked immediately." (a few seconds of audio)

The word often carries a slight sense of curiosity or incompleteness — you've seen or heard just enough to be intrigued, but not the full picture.

In technology and programming, a code snippet is a small, reusable block of code that performs one specific task. Programmers share snippets on forums, in documentation, or in tutorials. It's not a complete program — it's just the useful little chunk that solves a particular problem. For example, a snippet that shows how to reverse a string in Python.

In search engines, particularly Google, a featured snippet is the highlighted box that appears at the very top of your search results, sometimes even before any links. Google extracts a brief, relevant passage from a webpage — a snippet — and displays it directly so you can get your answer without clicking anywhere.
The tone and feel of the word

"Snippet" is casual and slightly informal in tone. It has a lightness to it. When someone gives you a snippet of information, they're not giving you a lecture or a report — they're giving you a quick taste.

It's also often used with the word "just" or "only" to reinforce how small it is: "I only heard a snippet" or "She shared just a snippet." This signals that the person wishes they had more, or that what was shared was deliberately brief.
How it compares to similar words

• A piece is broad and neutral — it doesn't tell you much about size or origin.
  • A fragment often implies something broken or incomplete, sometimes accidentally.
  • A excerpt is more formal and is almost exclusively used for written text.
  • A snippet sits in a sweet spot: casual, deliberately chosen, brief, and always implying it came from something bigger. It works across text, audio, video, and code — which makes it one of the most versatile words in this family.

• "I only heard a snippet of the conversation, so I don't know the full story."
  • "The artist released a 15-second snippet of her new album online."
  • "He pasted a code snippet into the chat to show us how the function works."
  • "Google showed a snippet from the NHS website right at the top of the results."
  • "The documentary is full of fascinating snippets from old interviews and archival footage."
  • "She gave me a few snippets of gossip but wouldn't tell me everything."

A snippet is a small, deliberately chosen piece taken from something larger — a brief extract that gives you a glimpse or taste without giving you the whole thing. It can apply to conversation, writing, audio, video, search results, or code.
14783: A snit is a state of irritation, agitation, or flustered annoyance — usually over something small or trivial. When someone is in a snit, they are worked up, flustered, and emotionally bothered, but not in a dramatic or deeply serious way. Think of it as the emotional version of a minor storm in a teacup.

Imagine someone planned a small dinner party and one guest showed up 10 minutes late. The host isn't devastated — but they're not fully calm either. They're quietly fuming, a little ruffled, visibly irritated, and perhaps making pointed comments under their breath. That inner state of petty agitation — that flustered, low-grade huff — is a snit.

It sits somewhere between mild annoyance and a small temper tantrum. It is not rage. It is not grief. It is not a full-blown argument. It is that particular uncomfortable emotional state where a person is bothered and perhaps slightly behaving like a child about it.
The key hidden layer: a touch of dismissiveness

This is crucial, and many learners miss it.

When you call someone's reaction a snit, you are gently implying that their upset is a bit disproportionate, petty, or unnecessary — that they're making more of something than it deserves. The word carries a mild, almost affectionate mockery. It subtly says: "You're upset, yes, but let's be honest — it's not that big a deal."

So if you say, "She's in a snit" rather than "She's very upset," you are quietly suggesting that her reaction is a little silly, a little overdone, perhaps even a little childish — without being outright rude about it.

This tone of gentle dismissal is baked into the word itself. It is what separates snit from words like fury or distress, which take the person's emotion fully seriously.

Snit is an informal word, used in everyday conversation. You would say it to a friend, a family member, or in casual writing — not in a formal report or a professional email.

It is used most commonly in American English. If you are speaking British English, people might not use this word as naturally, though they would understand it.

The most common pattern you will encounter is the phrase "in a snit":

"He's been in a snit all morning over that parking ticket."
"Don't get in a snit — it was just a joke."
"She worked herself into a snit because the coffee was cold."

You can also say someone "threw a snit" (meaning they had a small, irritated episode) or simply that they were "in a bit of a snit" (softening it even further).

• "My boss has been in a snit ever since the meeting didn't go his way."
    → He's been visibly irritated, touchy, and difficult to be around — over something relatively minor.
  • "She threw herself into a snit when she wasn't invited to the party."
    → She got worked up and sulky about it, perhaps more than the situation called for.
  • "Oh, ignore him — he's just in a snit because he lost the argument."
    → He's sulking and acting bothered. The speaker thinks it's not a serious reaction.
  • "Why are you in such a snit today? What happened?"
    → You seem flustered and irritable — what's the matter?
How it differs from similar words

FeelingWhat makes snit different

Anger is a broad word that can be serious and intense. A snit is always small-scale — you wouldn't describe someone who just lost a loved one as being "in a snit."

A tantrum is more explosive, more visible, and often associated with children. A snit is quieter and more internal — it's a simmering irritation rather than an outburst.

A huff is very close to a snit. If you're in a huff, you're sulking and offended. A snit is slightly more flustered and agitated, whereas a huff leans more toward sulking and wounded dignity. These two words can often be used interchangeably, though.

Pique (as in "a fit of pique") is similar and slightly more formal. A snit is more colloquial and folksy.
The full picture in one sentence
A snit is an informal word for a small, flustered state of irritation or agitation — with the quiet implication that the person's upset is a bit petty or more than the situation truly warranted.
14784: To snivel means to cry, whimper, or complain in a weak, pathetic, and self-pitying way — usually with sniffling and a runny nose involved. Think of a child who didn't get what they wanted and is now making a fuss about it in the most irritating, weepy way possible. That's sniveling.
The Two Sides of the Word

The verb snivel works on two levels that are tightly connected:

The physical side: Sniveling involves the actual, messy act of crying — with sniffling, a dripping nose, and whimpering. It's not clean, quiet, or dignified crying. It's the sloppy, noisy kind where someone can barely speak between sniffs.

The behavioral side: Sniveling also means to complain, whine, or moan about something in a feeble, self-pitying way — as if the person is a helpless victim who refuses to pull themselves together. Even without actual tears, someone can snivel just by whining and moaning pathetically.

In real use, these two sides often appear together — a person sniveling is typically both physically tearful and behaviorally pathetic at the same time.
The Crucial Part: What the Word Implies

This is where snivel becomes very interesting and precise. It is not a neutral word. It carries a strong sense of contempt and irritation from the person observing or describing the behavior.

When you say someone is sniveling, you are not just describing what they are doing — you are judging them for it. You are saying:

  • Their crying or complaining is not justified or is massively exaggerated.
  • They are being childishly weak and failing to show any backbone.
  • Their behavior is annoying and pitiable, not moving or sympathetic.
  • They are wallowing in self-pity instead of doing something useful.

This is a key distinction. If someone has lost a loved one and weeps deeply, you would never call that sniveling — that would be cruel and wrong. Sniveling is reserved for situations where the person's reaction seems weak, excessive, or unwarranted.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding snivel becomes much sharper when you place it next to related words:

Cry is completely neutral. It simply states a fact. "She cried at the movie." No judgment, no tone.

Weep is actually somewhat dignified. It suggests deep, genuine, heartfelt emotion. You weep for things that truly matter.

Sob is intense and genuine. A person sobbing is overwhelmed by real grief or pain. There's no mockery in calling someone's reaction "sobbing."

Whine is close to snivel but is more purely verbal — it focuses on complaining without necessarily involving tears. Snivel adds the physical, tearful, sniffly element on top of the whining quality.

Snivel sits at the lowest and most contemptuous end of this scale. It combines weakness, self-pity, tears, sniffling, and whining all at once — and it frames all of it as something unworthy of respect.
Who Uses This Word and When

Snivel is most commonly used when someone wants to tell another person — directly or indirectly — to stop being so pathetically weak and get on with things. It is frequently used:

  • By a stern or impatient person toward someone they think is overreacting: "Stop sniveling and get up."
  • To describe someone's behavior with obvious disapproval: "He spent the whole meeting sniveling about how unfair his workload was."
  • In a military, disciplinary, or tough-love context, where weakness is not tolerated.

It can be said directly to someone's face as a sharp command, or it can be used in the third person to describe someone behind their back — either way, the contempt is always present.

Snivel is not a word you'd find in a formal academic essay or an official report. It belongs to everyday spoken or written language, and it leans toward the informal side. You might find it in novels, conversation, opinion writing, or anywhere a writer wants to express contempt for weakness in a vivid and expressive way.
Putting It All Together With Examples

• "The soldier was told to stop sniveling and carry on with his duties." — Here the officer is dismissing the soldier's crying/complaining as unacceptable weakness.
  • "She sniveled into her sleeve, complaining that nobody ever helped her." — A picture of someone physically crying and sniffling while also whining and feeling sorry for themselves.
  • "I don't want to hear any more sniveling about how hard the exam was — everyone found it hard." — Used to shut down pathetic, self-pitying complaints.
  • "He sat in the corner sniveling while the rest of the team worked to fix the problem." — Paints someone as useless and weak while others show strength.

If you had to carry just one sentence in your memory, make it this: To snivel is to cry, sniffle, or complain in a weak and self-pitying way that other people find irritating, pathetic, and undeserving of sympathy.
14785:
A snob is a person who believes — consciously or not — that they are better than others, and who makes this belief visible through the way they treat people. They constantly rank human beings on an invisible scale of "superior" and "inferior," and they behave accordingly: looking down on those they consider beneath them, and eagerly flattering or admiring those they consider above them.

The word is always used as a criticism. Nobody proudly calls themselves a snob. When you call someone a snob, you are pointing out a flaw in their character.
The Two Directions a Snob Operates In

To truly understand a snob, you need to see that they operate in two directions simultaneously:

1. Downward — Contempt for the "inferior"
A snob treats people they consider lower (in wealth, status, education, taste, etc.) with coldness, dismissiveness, or barely hidden disrespect. They might ignore them, speak to them in a condescending tone, or simply act as if those people don't quite matter.

2. Upward — Admiration for the "superior"
At the same time, a snob eagerly seeks the approval of people they consider higher or more prestigious. They want to associate with the "right" people, attend the "right" events, and be seen in the "right" places.

This two-directional behaviour — looking down and looking up — is the hallmark of a snob.
What a Snob Bases Their Superiority On

Here is what makes the word flexible and widely applicable: a snob can base their sense of superiority on almost anything. It doesn't have to be wealth or social class. Whatever a person values deeply, they can become a snob about it.

  • Social/Class snob — Looks down on people with less money, a lower-status job, or a less prestigious background. They might subtly mock someone for taking public transport, or treat a waiter as an inconvenience rather than a person.
  • Intellectual snob — Looks down on people they consider less educated or less intelligent. They make others feel stupid for not knowing something, or they roll their eyes at "simple" or "popular" ideas.
  • Food snob — Dismisses people who eat "common" food. They act horrified if you enjoy fast food or instant noodles, and they cannot have a conversation about food without subtly implying that most people's tastes are unsophisticated.
  • Music snob — Looks down on people who listen to popular or mainstream music. They believe their taste (usually in obscure or classical music) is far superior, and they let people know it.
  • Literary snob — Dismisses readers of genre fiction, bestsellers, or "lowbrow" books. They only respect certain authors and make others feel embarrassed for what they read.
  • Wine snob / Coffee snob — Makes people feel inferior about what they drink. They turn a simple choice of beverage into a test of sophistication that most people are quietly expected to fail.

In every case, the structure is the same: I have refined taste / high status / superior knowledge, and you do not, and that makes me better than you.
How a Snob Behaves in Practice

Snobbery doesn't always look dramatic. It is often quiet and subtle. Here are some common behaviours:

  • Name-dropping: Casually mentioning prestigious people, brands, schools, or places they are connected to — not to share information, but to establish their status. ("Oh, I was just at the Tate Modern with the director last week...")
  • Condescending tone: Speaking to "lesser" people in a tone that is slightly too patient, as if they are explaining things to a child.
  • Visible disapproval: A small sigh, a raised eyebrow, or a brief pause when they hear your choice of music, restaurant, or holiday destination.
  • Excluding people: Deliberately making someone feel like an outsider — that they don't belong in a particular group, conversation, or space.
  • Praising the "right" things excessively: Going on at length about the superiority of certain brands, schools, art forms, or experiences — with the unspoken message being that people who cannot access these things are lacking.

• "Don't mind her — she's a terrible snob who refuses to eat at any restaurant that hasn't been reviewed in a magazine."
  • "He's an intellectual snob who makes you feel foolish for watching television."
  • "The new manager turned out to be a class snob; he was charming to the senior staff but barely acknowledged the junior employees."

• Snobbish / Snobby (adjective): Describing the behaviour or attitude. "She gave me a snobbish look when I mentioned where I went to school."
  • Snobbery (noun): The behaviour or quality of being a snob. "The snobbery in that club is insufferable."
  • Snobbishness (noun): Same as snobbery, slightly more formal. "His snobbishness drove most people away."
The Most Important Thing to Remember

The deepest truth about a snob is not just that they look down on people — it's that their sense of self-worth depends on feeling superior. A snob is not confident in themselves independently; they need a hierarchy, and they need to feel they are near the top of it. Remove the hierarchy, and the snob becomes insecure.

This is why snobbery is considered not just unpleasant but also somewhat pitiable by those who understand it well. The snob's contempt for others reveals, more than anything else, an anxiety about their own worth.
14786: "Snobbish" describes a person who believes they are better than others — and acts on that belief by looking down on people they consider inferior while eagerly admiring or trying to impress those they consider superior. It is always a negative word. Calling someone snobbish is a clear criticism of their attitude and behavior.

A snobbish person has two connected habits working at the same time, and understanding both is key.

Side one — looking down: They dismiss, disrespect, or ignore people they consider "beneath" them. They might do this with cold body language, rude remarks, or simply by refusing to engage with those people at all.

Side two — looking up: They are eager to associate with, impress, or name-drop people they consider "above" them. They become noticeably warmer and more attentive around high-status people.

Both sides come from the same root — an unhealthy obsession with rank, status, and the idea that some people are simply worth more than others.
What Do Snobbish People Judge Others On?

Snobbishness can appear in almost any area of life where people feel a sense of superiority.

Wealth and social class is the most classic form. A snobbish person might refuse to be friends with someone who is poor, who lives in an ordinary neighborhood, or who works what they consider a "low" job.

Education is another common one. A snobbish person might completely dismiss what someone says simply because they didn't attend a prestigious school or hold a university degree.

Taste and culture — this is where it gets subtle. A snobbish person might look down on others for enjoying popular music, mainstream movies, or fast food, while treating their own refined preferences as proof of their superiority. They might turn their nose up at something simply because it is popular or "common."

Intellect is yet another version. An intellectually snobbish person treats those they see as less intelligent as not worth their time — as if a conversation with an "ordinary" mind is beneath them.
The Most Important Nuance — Snobbishness Is About Attitude, Not Preference

This is the part most people miss, and getting it right is what separates a good understanding of this word from a shallow one.

Having high standards, refined tastes, or strong opinions does not make someone snobbish. A person who loves classical music, fine wine, or high-end fashion is not automatically snobbish. The snobbishness enters the picture the moment they begin to look down on, mock, or dismiss others for not sharing those tastes.

In other words, snobbishness is not about what you enjoy — it's about how you treat people who enjoy different things. A wine expert who enthusiastically shares their passion without making others feel small is not snobbish. A person who sneers at a friend for drinking cheap wine absolutely is.
How a Snobbish Person Typically Behaves

Because words alone don't paint the full picture, here's what snobbishness actually looks like in real life.

A snobbish person might speak to certain people in a condescending tone — slow, over-explained, as if the other person is not intelligent enough to keep up. They might name-drop prestigious schools, exclusive clubs, or important people in conversation to signal how elevated their social circle is. They might judge someone instantly based on surface things — what clothes they wear, what phone they use, what neighborhood they come from — before a word has even been exchanged. In a group setting, they might become visibly more interested and engaged the moment someone important or high-status walks in, while the "ordinary" people in the room simply fade from their attention.

Being on the receiving end of snobbish behavior feels deeply humiliating. It makes a person feel judged and found unworthy — not because of anything they did wrong, but simply because of who they are, where they come from, or what they can or cannot afford. That is precisely why "snobbish" is such a strong criticism and why the word carries genuine negativity.

Arrogant means having an inflated sense of one's own importance. A snobbish person is a specific kind of arrogant — one whose arrogance is rooted in social status, class, or taste. All snobbish people are arrogant, but not all arrogant people are snobbish.

Condescending means speaking to others as if they are less intelligent or less important than you. Snobbish people are typically condescending, but condescension can exist without snobbishness. A snobbish person is condescending for social or status-based reasons specifically.

Elitist is the closest neighbor. It refers to the belief that certain people are inherently superior and deserve more power or privilege. Elitism is the broader ideology; snobbishness is the personal, everyday attitude and behavior that flows from it. Someone who is snobbish in their daily interactions is essentially acting out elitist beliefs in real life.

"She refused to speak to the new employee — her snobbish attitude was obvious to everyone in the room."

"He was deeply snobbish about literature, dismissing anyone who enjoyed popular fiction as intellectually lazy."

"Growing up in a wealthy family made her snobbish without her even realizing it — she simply could not relate to anyone who hadn't had the same privileges."

"The restaurant had a snobbish atmosphere that made ordinary guests feel unwelcome the moment they walked in."

Snob is the noun — the person. "He's a snob."
Snobbery is the noun for the behavior or attitude itself. "The snobbery in that office was exhausting."
Snobbishly is the adverb. "She snobbishly walked past without acknowledging him."
Snobbishness is the noun for the quality or state of being snobbish. "His snobbishness cost him many friendships."

A snobbish person believes some people are simply worth more than others — based on wealth, class, education, or taste — and treats people accordingly, with contempt for those "below" and admiration for those "above."
14787: Snobby describes a person who believes they are better than others — and who actually shows this belief through the way they talk, act, or treat people. A snobby person doesn't just quietly feel superior; they make others feel inferior, often without saying it directly.
What a Snobby Person Actually Does

A snobby person:

  • Looks down on others who they think are less wealthy, less educated, less stylish, or less cultured than themselves.
  • Acts cold, dismissive, or uninterested toward people they consider "below" them. They might not greet someone, give short replies, or simply ignore them.
  • Is easily impressed by status — things like expensive brands, prestigious schools, famous names, or high social positions. They quickly warm up to people with status and quickly cool down toward those without it.
  • Judges people for their choices in ways that feel unkind — for example, quietly mocking someone for the food they eat, the music they like, the clothes they wear, or the place they grew up.
  • Talks about themselves or their world in a way that excludes others — name-dropping expensive restaurants, mentioning elite schools, or referencing experiences that only wealthy or privileged people would have, as if everyone should relate to this.
The Key Feeling Behind "Snobby"

The heart of "snobby" is a mix of two things happening at once:

  1. A feeling of personal superiority — "I am better, more refined, more sophisticated than you."
  2. A display of that feeling — acting in a way that makes others feel small, unwelcome, or judged.

A person can be snobby without saying a single rude word. A glance, a raised eyebrow, a cold silence, or a subtle smirk can all be snobby. It's about an attitude that comes through, not just spoken words.
Different Areas Where Someone Can Be Snobby

Snobbiness is not limited to wealth or social class. A person can be snobby about almost anything they feel superior in:

  • Social class / money: Looks down on people who are less wealthy or from a "lower" background. Might refuse to socialize with someone because they don't live in the "right" neighborhood or went to the "wrong" school.
  • Education / intelligence: Treats people as lesser for not having a university degree, or for not knowing about philosophy, literature, or science. Might correct others in a condescending way.
  • Food / drink: Dismisses people who eat simple or popular food. ("You drink instant coffee? I only drink single-origin, hand-roasted beans.")
  • Art, music, or film: Looks down on people who enjoy popular movies, pop music, or mainstream entertainment. ("You liked that film? It was so shallow.")
  • Fashion / brands: Judges people based on whether their clothes or accessories are expensive or designer.
  • Accent or dialect: Acts as though a certain way of speaking is "proper" and others are inferior.

The subject changes, but the attitude is always the same: "I have refined taste / superior knowledge / better background — and you don't."
The Crucial Difference: Snobby vs. Simply Having Preferences

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Having preferences or high standards is NOT the same as being snobby.

  • A person who personally prefers classical music but enjoys talking to someone who loves pop music → not snobby.
  • A person who prefers classical music and makes the pop music fan feel stupid or uncultured for their taste → snobby.

The difference is not what you like. It's whether you use your preferences as a weapon to rank people. A snobby person doesn't just prefer things — they use those preferences to build a wall between themselves and people they consider inferior.

You can have the most sophisticated taste in the world and be completely warm, humble, and welcoming. That is not snobby. Snobbery begins the moment you start treating others as lesser beings because of what they like, where they come from, or what they have.
What It Feels Like to Be on the Receiving End

When a person is snobby toward you, you typically feel:

  • Looked down upon or judged — as if you said or did something wrong just by being yourself.
  • Unwelcome or excluded — as if you don't belong in their company.
  • Self-conscious or small — questioning your own choices, background, or worth.
  • Dismissed — as if your presence or opinion doesn't really matter to them.

This is why "snobby" is a negative word. It's not simply describing someone with high standards. It's describing someone whose behavior makes others feel inferior, disrespected, or invisible.
Degree and Intensity

"Snobby" can apply to mild or strong versions of this behavior:

  • Mildly snobby: Someone who is a little bit aloof about their taste in wine and gently wrinkles their nose at cheap brands, but doesn't go out of their way to make others feel bad.
  • Very snobby: Someone who openly mocks others' choices, refuses to engage with people they consider beneath them, and constantly signals their own superiority.

The word "snobby" covers the whole range, though it always implies a negative judgment of the person being described.
How It's Used in Sentences

• "She was so snobby at the party — she wouldn't even talk to anyone who didn't go to a private school."
  • "Don't be snobby about food. Not everyone can afford to eat at fancy restaurants."
  • "He's a bit snobby about books. If you haven't read the classics, he acts like you're not worth his time."
  • "I expected the staff at that boutique to be snobby, but they were actually very friendly."
  • "Growing up wealthy made her snobby without her even realizing it."
Related Words (Same Family)

• Snob (noun) — the person who behaves this way. "He's such a snob."
  • Snobbishly (adverb) — describes how someone does something with this attitude. "She snobbishly refused to sit at our table."
  • Snobbery / snobbishness (noun) — the quality or behavior itself. "His snobbery made him very unpopular."
  • Snobbish (adjective) — a slightly more formal version of snobby, meaning exactly the same thing.
Words That Mean the Opposite

To fully understand "snobby," it helps to know its opposites:

  • Down-to-earth — treats everyone as an equal, regardless of background or status.
  • Humble — doesn't think of themselves as better than others.
  • Unpretentious — doesn't try to seem more sophisticated or important than they are.
  • Warm or welcoming — makes people feel included and valued.
A One-Line Summary

If you had to boil it down to one sentence:

A snobby person acts superior to others and makes those they consider "beneath" them feel judged, unwelcome, or small — based on things like money, taste, education, or social class.
14788: Someone who is snooty believes they are better than other people — better in terms of wealth, social class, taste, or refinement — and they show this belief through cold, dismissive, or superior behavior toward others. It's not just an internal feeling of pride; snooty people make others feel looked down upon.
The Attitude Behind It

A snooty person carries a quiet (sometimes not so quiet) contempt for people they see as being below their level. They treat someone differently depending on how "important," wealthy, educated, or cultured they think that person is. If you don't meet their standard, they simply act as though you're not worth their full attention or respect.

Think of it this way: a snooty person has an invisible scale in their head, and they're constantly measuring whether you're worthy of being treated warmly.
How It Looks in Real Life

Snooty behavior can show up in many ways:

  • Giving someone a cold, barely-there greeting while being warm and friendly to someone else they consider more "important"
  • Speaking in a dismissive or bored tone, as if talking to you is a waste of their time
  • Turning up their nose at your choices — where you shop, what you eat, what music you like, or where you went to school
  • Making comments that subtly (or not so subtly) put you down
  • Refusing to mix with people they consider "ordinary" or beneath them
  • Acting as though certain restaurants, brands, neighborhoods, or events are simply too low-class for them

A snooty waiter, for example, might ignore a casually dressed customer while fussing over someone in an expensive suit. A snooty classmate might roll their eyes when you mention your favorite TV show, as if only people with poor taste would watch it.
Key Examples in Sentences

• "The receptionist at the luxury hotel was so snooty — she looked us up and down before even saying hello."
  • "He can be very snooty about wine. If it's not expensive, he won't drink it."
  • "I didn't feel welcome in that shop. The staff had a snooty attitude the entire time."
  • "She gave a snooty little laugh when I told her I took the bus to work."
  • "Don't be snooty about other people's reading choices — not everyone has to read literary fiction."
  • "The school has a reputation for being snooty — they only seem to care about students from wealthy families."
What Makes Someone Snooty

Snootiness usually comes from one or more of these things:

  • Wealth — having money (or wanting to appear to)
  • Social class — belonging (or trying to belong) to an upper-class background
  • Education — having studied at prestigious schools and looking down on those who haven't
  • Taste — thinking one's preferences in food, art, fashion, or culture are superior
  • Status — holding a high professional or social position

Crucially, a person doesn't have to actually be wealthy or elite to be snooty. Some people who have very little act snooty because they want to be seen as refined or above others. The attitude is what makes someone snooty, not necessarily their real circumstances.
What Snooty Does NOT Mean

Snooty ≠ Shy or Reserved
A shy person is quiet or withdrawn because they feel nervous or unsure. A snooty person is cold or dismissive because they think they're too good for you. The difference is the reason: insecurity vs. a sense of superiority.

Snooty ≠ Simply Rude
A rude person is unpleasant to everyone. A snooty person is selectively unpleasant — they treat people differently based on perceived status. They can be perfectly charming to someone they consider important, while being cold and dismissive to someone they see as beneath them. That selectivity is the hallmark of snootiness.

Snooty ≠ Having High Standards
Having high standards for quality is not snooty in itself. What makes it snooty is when you look down on and dismiss people who don't share or meet those standards. For example, preferring organic food is a personal choice. Sneering at a friend for eating fast food and acting like they're beneath you — that's snooty.
Can Things (Not Just People) Be Snooty?

Yes, though less commonly. When we describe a place or thing as snooty, we mean it has the feel of a snooty person — exclusive, cold, and unwelcoming to anyone who doesn't fit a certain image.

  • "That club has a snooty atmosphere — the bouncers judge you by what you're wearing."
  • "The magazine has a snooty tone, as if it's writing only for the ultra-rich."
How It Feels to Be on the Receiving End

When a snooty person interacts with you, you typically feel:

  • Put down or made to feel "not good enough"
  • Judged for your background, clothes, accent, or tastes
  • Unwelcome, like you don't belong
  • Invisible or unimportant

This is why "snooty" is almost always used as a negative word. Nobody sees being called snooty as a compliment.
Register and Tone of the Word

"Snooty" is an informal word. You'd use it in everyday conversation and casual writing. It carries a slightly playful or critical edge — when someone calls a person snooty, they're gently (or not so gently) criticizing that behavior.

In formal or academic writing, you would more likely use words like condescending, supercilious, disdainful, or haughty instead.
Words Close in Meaning

• Snobby / snobbish — the closest synonyms; a snob looks down on those of "lower" class or taste (snooty and snobby are nearly interchangeable in everyday use)
  • Stuck-up — informal; acting as if you're too good for others
  • Condescending — treating others as if they're less intelligent or important than you
  • Haughty — proud, cold, and disdainful
  • Arrogant — an exaggerated belief in one's own importance (broader than snooty; doesn't always involve class)
  • Supercilious — formal; showing contemptuous superiority
Opposite Words

• Down-to-earth — unpretentious, friendly regardless of status
  • Humble — modest, doesn't think of oneself as superior
  • Approachable — easy and comfortable to talk to
  • Unpretentious — not trying to appear more important or refined than one is
A Quick Mental Image to Remember It

Imagine a person at a party who greets a well-dressed guest with a warm smile, then turns to look at a casually dressed stranger with a cool, barely-there nod before slowly turning away. They didn't say anything openly rude — but the message was clear: "You're not on my level."

That person is snooty.

A snorkel is a breathing tube — a hollow, tube-shaped device that lets a person breathe air while their face is underwater.

Think of it this way: normally, if you put your face in water, you can't breathe. A snorkel solves this problem by creating a path for air — from above the water's surface, all the way to your mouth — so you can breathe while looking down into the water.

A snorkel is typically a curved or J-shaped tube, roughly 30–40 cm (about 12–16 inches) long. It has two ends:

  • The mouthpiece — the bottom end, which goes into your mouth (between your teeth and lips, like biting down gently on it).
  • The open top — the upper end, which sticks up out of the water into the open air.

It's usually made of plastic or rubber, and it often attaches to the side of a swimming mask (the glass-fronted mask that covers your eyes and nose) so it stays in place hands-free.

Many modern snorkels also have a splash guard or a special valve at the top. This prevents water from accidentally spilling in when a small wave comes along, and it lets you easily blow out any water that does enter.

The concept is beautifully simple:

  1. You put on a swimming mask and grip the snorkel's mouthpiece in your mouth.
  2. You float face-down on the surface of the water.
  3. The tube extends upward, with its open top poking above the water's surface.
  4. You breathe normally — air travels down the tube as you inhale, and your breath travels up and out as you exhale.

As long as the top of the tube stays above the water, you have a continuous supply of fresh air, even though your face is submerged.
What It Allows You to Do

A snorkel allows you to observe the underwater world — coral reefs, fish, sea turtles, and other marine life — without needing to hold your breath or surface every few seconds for air. You can float calmly for many minutes, face-down, breathing steadily, watching everything below you as if through a window.

This activity is called snorkeling (the verb form), and it is one of the most popular and accessible water activities in the world. It doesn't require special training or heavy equipment — just the mask, the snorkel, and a pair of fins (flippers for your feet, used for propulsion).

A snorkel is only useful at the surface. If you dive deeper — even a meter or two below the surface — the top of the tube goes underwater too, and you can no longer breathe through it. At that point, you must hold your breath (which some snorkelers do, briefly, to get a closer look at something below, then return to the surface).

This is the key difference between snorkeling (breathing through a tube at the surface) and scuba diving (carrying a tank of compressed air on your back to breathe at any depth). A snorkel is not a substitute for a scuba tank — it is a surface tool.

The word "snorkel" also refers to a device on a submarine — and this is the second major meaning of the noun.

A submarine normally runs on diesel engines when on the surface. When it dives below the surface, it switches to battery-powered electric motors, because diesel engines need air to run and exhaust fumes must escape.

The submarine snorkel (also spelled snort in British naval terminology) is a retractable tube system that can be extended up through the water to just above the surface. This allows the submarine to:

  1. Draw in fresh air to run its diesel engines — even while remaining mostly submerged.
  2. Expel exhaust gases back out through the tube.
  3. Recharge its batteries using those diesel engines, without needing to fully surface.

This is enormously valuable in wartime or stealth situations, because a submarine using its snorkel is much harder to detect than one that has fully surfaced. It allows the submarine to stay hidden while still powering up.

A third (less common but real) use of the word: some military vehicles, particularly tanks and armored personnel carriers, are fitted with a snorkel — a tube extension that attaches to the vehicle's air intake. This allows the vehicle to drive through deep water (river crossings, for example) while still getting the air its engine needs to run. Without the snorkel, the engine would stall underwater due to lack of air.

• "She put the snorkel in her mouth, dipped her face into the warm lagoon, and gasped at the explosion of colorful fish below her."
  • "The submarine raised its snorkel and began recharging its batteries under cover of darkness."
  • "He forgot to clear the water from his snorkel before breathing in, and inhaled a mouthful of seawater."
  • "The tank was fitted with a snorkel so it could cross the river without stalling."

ContextWhat the snorkel does
Swimming / recreationLets a person breathe while floating face-down on the water's surface
SubmarineLets a submerged submarine run its diesel engines and recharge batteries
Military vehicleLets a vehicle's engine breathe air while crossing deep water

The unifying idea across all three meanings is the same: a snorkel is always a tube that carries air from above the surface to something that needs to breathe below it.
